### 64. Inheritance · Medium

*lld · gate confidence 0.8*

<sub>to object to this card: `## lld-inheritance` then `match: Match each language or mechanism with the guarantee it provi`</sub>

**Question**

Match each language or mechanism with the guarantee it provides for inheritance.

**Options**

**Left**: Java and C#, C++, JavaScript, Go
**Right**: Prototype delegation, Multiple base classes with virtual inheritance, Struct embedding, Single class inheritance with multiple interfaces

**Answer (the reader is graded on)**

- 0 ↔ 3 · 1 ↔ 1 · 2 ↔ 0 · 3 ↔ 2

**Reference answer**

Java and C# guarantee single class inheritance with multiple interface implementation, avoiding the diamond problem for classes. C++ supports multiple base classes and uses virtual inheritance to share a single base subobject in a diamond. JavaScript's class syntax is prototype delegation, where objects inherit directly from other objects. Go uses struct embedding, which provides field and method promotion without class inheritance.

**Graded on**

- Java and C# allow one base class but many interfaces.
- C++ permits multiple base classes; virtual inheritance resolves diamond ambiguity.
- JavaScript classes are syntactic sugar over prototype delegation.
- Go struct embedding promotes fields and methods without creating a class hierarchy.

<details><summary>The lesson this came from</summary>

Inheritance is a mechanism by which a derived class acquires the fields and methods of a base class and can override or extend them. It establishes a subtype relationship, so a base-class reference can refer to a derived object. In Java and C#, a class can inherit from one base class but implement many interfaces; C++ permits multiple base classes. JavaScript's class syntax is prototype delegation under the hood, while Go uses struct embedding rather than class inheritance.

## Why interviewers ask this

Interviewers ask this to see whether you understand the mechanics beyond a UML arrow: constructor order, dynamic dispatch, overload hiding, and the conditions under which inheritance is the right design. They are also probing whether you reach for composition before inheritance when the relationship is not substitutable, which is a common LLD failure.

## The core idea

The core mechanism is not just copying members: an object stores a base subobject, and lookup/dispatch rules decide which member is used. Constructor order runs base-to-derived, and in Java a constructor may defer to another constructor in the same class via this before the chain eventually calls super. At compile time, the declared type and visible names determine which overload applies; at runtime, the object's dynamic type selects the override for virtual methods. That separation explains common bugs such as C++ name hiding and uninitialized fields when an overridden method is called from a base constructor. Because inheritance creates a tight, single-hierarchy coupling, it should be used for substitutability, while composition is preferred for reuse.

## Key points

- Inheritance creates an is-a relation by reusing a base class's fields and methods, but constructors are not inherited.
- In Java, base-class constructors run before derived-class constructors, and a derived constructor's first statement may be super(...), this(...), or an implicit super() when an accessible no-arg base constructor exists.
- For virtual methods, dispatch chooses the override by the object's runtime type, while overload resolution chooses by static argument types and visible names.
- In C++, a derived-class function with the same name hides all base-class overloads unless the derived class contains using Base::name;.
- Composition is usually safer for code reuse because inheritance couples the subclass to a base implementation and limits it to one base class in Java and C#.

## Your 60-second answer

Inheritance is when a subclass derives fields and methods from a superclass, creating an is-a relationship so a reference to the superclass can hold a subclass instance. The subclass reuses base behavior and can override selected methods. In Java and C#, a class may extend one base class but implement many interfaces; C++ allows multiple base classes. Constructor execution runs the base constructor before the derived constructor, and in Java the first statement can be super, another constructor of the same class via this, or an implicit super call when a no-argument base constructor is accessible. At runtime, overridden virtual calls dispatch to the object's runtime type. The trade-off is coupling: the derived class depends on the base class's representation and behavior, so for mere code reuse composition is often the better choice.

## If they dig deeper

**When would you use inheritance instead of composition?**

Use inheritance when a true is-a relationship exists and you want substitutability: a Dog should be usable wherever Animal is expected. Use composition when you only need to reuse behavior; composition keeps the wrapper class in control, avoids base class coupling, and allows changing the reused component at runtime. In LLD, composition is usually the default.

**What is constructor execution order in Java and C++?**

Java and C++ both run base-class constructors before derived-class constructors. In Java the first statement of a constructor is either super(...), this(...), or an implicit super() when there is an accessible no-arg superclass constructor; this-chains must eventually reach super(...). C++ constructs base subobjects first, then member objects in declaration order, then the derived constructor body.

**Why is calling an overridable method from a constructor dangerous?**

A base-class constructor may invoke an overridden method before the derived class's fields are initialized. In Java and C#, the call dispatches to the derived override, so it can read null or default fields; in C++, during a base constructor the dynamic type is still base, so it calls the base implementation instead. Therefore constructors should only call private or final methods, or avoid virtual calls.

**What is the diamond problem, and how do different languages handle it?**

If B and C inherit from A and D inherits from both B and C, there are two A subobjects, creating ambiguity about which A's fields and methods D uses. C++ supports multiple inheritance and resolves this with virtual inheritance so B and C share a single A subobject; Java and C# do not allow multiple class inheritance, but allow multiple interface inheritance. Python allows multiple inheritance and resolves method lookup with the MRO (C3 linearization).

**What does the Liskov Substitution Principle require of inheritance?**

Subtypes must be substitutable for their base type without altering correctness: overridden methods must not strengthen preconditions or weaken postconditions, and must preserve invariants. Violations like a square that rejects width changes while overriding setWidth from a rectangle show a bad is-a relationship, so composition or a different abstraction is better.

## Worked example

Consider three Java classes: Base prints 'B' in its no-arg constructor; Derived has constructors Derived() { this(7); System.out.print("D "); } and Derived(int x) { super(); System.out.print("D(" + x + ") "); }. Executing new Derived() calls this(7), then super(), so output is B D(7) D. If Derived overrides void report(), a call Base b = new Derived(); b.report(); runs the Derived override because the runtime type of the object is Derived, even though the declared type is Base. An overloaded report(int n) inherited from Base remains callable on Derived, but a same-name method in Derived would hide all base overloads in C++ unless a using declaration is present.

## Common traps

- Treating inheritance as the default way to reuse code without checking whether a subclass is substitutable for its base; this makes future changes break subclasses.
- Assuming constructors are inherited; each subclass must define constructors and, in Java and C++, ensure the base subobject is constructed.
- Forgetting that C++ non-virtual methods do not use runtime dispatch, so calls through a base pointer execute the base implementation even if a derived function has the same signature.
- Calling overridable methods from constructors and relying on derived fields, which leads to null or uninitialized reads in Java and C#.

</details>

### 65. Probability and Statistics · Easy

*ai · gate confidence 0.7*

<sub>to object to this card: `## ai-probability-and-statistics` then `match: Sort each statement into the bucket that best describes it: `</sub>

**Question**

Sort each statement into the bucket that best describes it: Probability, Statistics, or Both. Each statement belongs to exactly one bucket.

**Options**

**Items**: Assigns a number in [0,1] to events under a model of randomness, Uses observed data to infer properties of the generating process, The Law of Large Numbers describes convergence of sample means, A confidence interval is a procedure with long-run frequency properties, Bayes' rule can update beliefs about parameters, Maximum likelihood estimation is used in machine learning
**Columns**: Probability, Statistics, Both

**Answer (the reader is graded on)**

- 0 ↔ 0 · 1 ↔ 1 · 2 ↔ 0 · 3 ↔ 1 · 4 ↔ 2 · 5 ↔ 2

**Reference answer**

Probability: 'Assigns a number in [0,1] to events under a model of randomness', 'The Law of Large Numbers describes convergence of sample means'. Statistics: 'Uses observed data to infer properties of the generating process', 'A confidence interval is a procedure with long-run frequency properties'. Both: 'Bayes' rule can update beliefs about parameters', 'Maximum likelihood estimation is used in machine learning'.

**Graded on**

- Probability goes from model to data; statistics goes from data to model.
- LLN is a probability result about random variables, not an inference procedure.
- Confidence intervals are frequentist statistical procedures.
- Bayes' rule and MLE are used in both probability and statistics.

<details><summary>The lesson this came from</summary>

Probability assigns a number in [0,1] to events under a model of randomness; statistics inverts this by using observed data to infer properties of the process that generated it. In machine learning, probability supplies the language for uncertainty, likelihoods, priors, and loss functions, while statistical inference covers estimation and hypothesis testing. The word inference also has a second meaning in ML systems: the forward pass of a trained model on new inputs, distinct from training.

## Why interviewers ask this

Interviewers use probability questions to test whether you can model a random process precisely, define the sample space, and avoid double-counting or independence errors. Statistics questions probe whether you can choose an estimator, interpret a likelihood, and state what a confidence interval does and does not mean. For ML roles they also check whether you understand how objective functions relate to maximum likelihood or Bayesian updating.

## The core idea

Probability is a function from events to [0,1]; discrete events use a probability mass function that sums to 1, and continuous variables use a density whose integral over an interval gives probability. Likelihood is a function of the model parameters for fixed observed data and is not a probability distribution over parameters. Frequentist inference treats parameters as fixed unknown constants and relies on long-run frequency properties of estimators; Bayesian inference treats parameters as random variables and updates a prior to a posterior via Bayes' rule. The Law of Large Numbers says that as a sample grows, the sample mean of i.i.d. variables approaches the population mean, and the Central Limit Theorem says its standardized form tends toward a standard normal distribution. For interview calculations, define the sample space and count equally likely outcomes only when they truly are equally likely, then use inclusion-exclusion to handle overlaps.

## Key points

- For a finite sample space of equally likely outcomes, probability is the count of favorable outcomes divided by total outcomes; for a continuous variable, probability is the integral of the PDF over an interval.
- Likelihood L(θ|x)=P(x|θ) is a function of θ for fixed observed x and is not a probability distribution over θ; maximum likelihood selects the parameter that makes the observed data most probable.
- The Law of Large Numbers says the sample mean of independent and identically distributed variables converges to the population mean as sample size grows; the Central Limit Theorem says its standardized form approaches a standard normal distribution.
- Frequentist inference treats parameters as fixed unknown constants and uses long-run frequency properties of estimators; Bayesian inference treats parameters as random variables and updates prior to posterior via Bayes' rule.
- Many ML loss functions are negative log-likelihoods: cross-entropy for classification corresponds to the negative log-likelihood of a categorical distribution, and L2 regularization corresponds to a Gaussian prior in a maximum-a-posteriori interpretation.

## Your 60-second answer

Probability gives a formal language for uncertainty: an event gets a number between 0 and 1, and for equally likely outcomes it's favorable over total outcomes. Statistics inverts that direction. Instead of going from model to data, we go from observed data back to the model, using estimators like maximum likelihood or Bayesian updating. A key distinction is that likelihood is a function of the model parameters for fixed data, not a probability over parameters. Frequentists treat the parameter as a fixed unknown and rely on long-run frequencies; Bayesians place a prior on it and update to a posterior. In ML, this shows up everywhere: cross-entropy loss is negative log-likelihood, and regularization encodes prior information. The main trade-off is that Bayesian methods give more interpretable uncertainty but require a prior and are often more computationally expensive than point estimates.

## If they dig deeper

**What is the difference between a PMF and a PDF?**

A probability mass function gives P(X=x) for each value of a discrete variable and sums to 1 over all values. A probability density function gives density for a continuous variable; the probability of an interval is the integral of the PDF over that interval, and the probability of any single point is 0.

**How do probability and likelihood differ?**

Probability describes the chance of data given fixed parameters and sums to 1 over all possible data. Likelihood is a function of parameters for fixed observed data and does not integrate or sum to 1 over parameters; it is used to compare parameter values, not to assign posterior probability by itself.

**How do frequentist and Bayesian approaches differ in parameter estimation?**

Frequentists treat parameters as fixed unknown constants and estimate them with methods like MLE, with uncertainty coming from the sampling distribution over repeated samples. Bayesians treat parameters as random variables with a prior distribution, then update to a posterior using Bayes' rule, which gives direct probability statements about the parameters.

**What is the connection between maximum likelihood estimation and cross-entropy loss?**

For i.i.d. data, MLE chooses parameters that maximize the likelihood, so minimizing negative log-likelihood. For classification with categorical targets, cross-entropy loss is exactly the negative log-likelihood of the one-hot target under the model's predicted probability distribution.

**Why can't you say a 95% frequentist confidence interval has a 95% probability of containing the true parameter after you compute it?**

Under frequentism the parameter is a fixed value, so the specific interval either contains it or it does not. The 95% property is about the procedure over repeated random samples, not about the parameter after observing one interval. A direct probability statement about the parameter requires a Bayesian credible interval with a specified prior.

## Worked example

For 30 people in a room, assume birthdays are independent and uniformly distributed across 365 days. The total number of birthday assignments is 365^30. For all birthdays to be distinct, person 1 has 365 choices, person 2 has 364, and so on down to person 30 having 336, so the number of distinct-birthday assignments is 365×364×...×336, written 365P30. The probability is therefore (365×364×...×336) / 365^30, which equals the product ∏_{i=0}^{29}(365−i)/365. This product is about 0.294. For 23 people the same no-match product is about 0.493, so the probability of at least one shared birthday is about 0.507. The threshold seems small because 23 people create C(23,2)=253 possible pairs that could match.

## Common traps

- Adding probabilities of overlapping events without subtracting the intersection, as in the two-consecutive-threes dice problem, causes double-counting.
- Treating likelihood as a probability distribution over parameters, which leads to invalid normalization and conflates MLE with a posterior mode.
- Using combinations instead of permutations in birthday problems when assignments of distinct birthdays to specific people matter, which changes the denominator of the probability.
- Interpreting a frequentist confidence interval as a Bayesian credible interval after the data are observed.

</details>

### 66. Choosing and organizing stories · Medium

*behavioral · gate confidence 0.8*

<sub>to object to this card: `## beh-choosing-and-organizing-stories` then `match: Sort each story-preparation practice into the bucket that be`</sub>

**Question**

Sort each story-preparation practice into the bucket that best describes it. Assume the candidate is preparing for a standard behavioral interview and wants a reusable story bank.

**Options**

**Items**: Preparing one story per expected question, Selecting 3–5 projects with high impact, complexity, and personal involvement, Writing each project as a STAR/R narrative, Choosing projects by company prestige rather than personal involvement, Treating STAR/R as a fixed script, Identifying distinct behaviors within each story so it can be reoriented, Keeping the set small to practice deeply, De-identifying confidential details while keeping technical depth
**Columns**: Builds a reusable story bank, Undermines a reusable story bank, Neutral or situational

**Answer (the reader is graded on)**

- 0 ↔ 1 · 1 ↔ 0 · 2 ↔ 0 · 3 ↔ 1 · 4 ↔ 1 · 5 ↔ 0 · 6 ↔ 2 · 7 ↔ 2

**Reference answer**

The practices that build a reusable story bank are: selecting 3–5 projects with high impact, complexity, and personal involvement; writing each as a STAR/R narrative; and identifying distinct behaviors within each story so it can be reoriented to different questions. The practices that undermine it are: preparing one story per expected question, choosing projects by company prestige rather than personal involvement, and treating STAR/R as a fixed script. The remaining practices are neutral or situational: keeping the set small to practice deeply is good, but only if the stories are well-developed; de-identifying confidential details is fine, but only if you can still describe your own actions; and mapping one story to different questions is good, but only if you lead with the targeted behavior rather than reciting the whole story.

**Graded on**

- A reusable story bank comes from 3–5 well-developed projects, not one anecdote per question.
- Each story should be a STAR/R narrative with emphasis on Actions.
- A single substantial project can answer multiple behavioral questions if its distinct behaviors are identified.
- Practices that reduce reusability include over-scripting, choosing stories by prestige, and ignoring personal involvement.

<details><summary>The lesson this came from</summary>

Choosing and organizing stories is the preparation step where you inventory specific past work situations, select a small set of 3–5 projects, and reduce each to a structured narrative: Situation, Task, Action, Result, and optionally Reflection. The goal is a reusable story bank, not a script for every possible question. Each story captures repeatable behaviors rather than just outcomes.

## Why interviewers ask this

Interviewers use behavioral questions to sample past behavior as evidence of future behavior. A candidate who has organized reusable stories can answer many different questions from the same project, because each substantial project usually contains ambiguity, conflict, communication, and execution. Interviewers are testing whether you can produce concrete, personal actions under pressure rather than generic claims.

## The core idea

Most behavioral answers come from a small set of well-developed projects, not one unique anecdote per question. Pick 3–5 projects with high impact, high complexity, and high personal involvement. Spread them across four categories: high-impact launches or refactors, challenging situations such as tight deadlines or failures, leadership moments, and learning experiences from mistakes. For each project, write a STAR/R story and focus on the Actions, because those are the repeatable behaviors the interview is named after. One story can then be reoriented to answer questions about conflict, ambiguity, influence, or failure depending on which part of the narrative the question targets.

## Key points

- Collect 3–5 past projects that had high impact, high complexity, and high involvement by you personally.
- Choose stories across four categories: high-impact launches or refactors, challenging situations, leadership moments, and learning experiences.
- Write each project as a STAR/R narrative: Situation, Task, Action, Result, with optional Reflection.
- The Actions are the key evidence because interviews evaluate repeatable behaviors, not past project outcomes.
- A single substantial project can often answer multiple behavioral questions because it contains ambiguity, conflict, communication, and execution.

## Your 60-second answer

If I'm preparing, I first go through my resume, performance reviews, and project history and pick three to five projects where I personally had significant involvement, the work was complex, and the outcome mattered. I intentionally spread them across four categories: a major launch or refactor, a challenging situation like a tight deadline or production failure, a leadership or cross-team effort, and a mistake I learned from. For each, I write a STAR/R story: Situation, Task, Action, Result, and sometimes a short reflection. The Actions matter most because interviewers are looking for behaviors they can expect from me on their team, not just what the project achieved. The trade-off is maintenance: I keep the set small because three well-developed stories are more adaptable than twenty shallow ones.

## If they dig deeper

**How many stories do you prepare, and why that number?**

Three to five is enough to cover the common behavioral themes while still being small enough to practice deeply. Most questions can be answered by reorienting one of those projects, so a larger set just dilutes preparation.

**How do you decide which projects become stories?**

I filter for impact, complexity, and personal involvement first. Then I check coverage: at least one major launch or refactor, one challenging failure or conflict, one leadership moment, and one learning experience from a mistake.

**What does the extra R in STAR/R add?**

The reflection shows what changed in your approach after the result. It turns a project recap into evidence of learning and self-correction, which is closer to the repeatable behavior the interviewer is assessing.

**How do you map one story to different questions?**

I identify the distinct behaviors in each story: handling ambiguity, resolving conflict, influencing without authority, recovering from failure. When a question targets one of those, I lead with that phase of the story and compress the rest.

**What if your best project was highly confidential or mostly a team effort?**

I de-identify details but keep the technical depth, and I describe my specific decisions and actions rather than the team's. If I cannot point to my own behaviors, I choose a less impressive project where I had more control.

## Worked example

An engineer preparing might choose a six-week migration to a new message queue they led. The situation was that the old queue dropped messages under peak load, and the task was to migrate without stopping writes. Their actions included writing a dual-write adapter, coordinating with three downstream teams, and rolling back once after a serialization bug. The result was a completed migration with less manual intervention, and the reflection notes that earlier load testing would have caught the bug. This same story can answer a conflict question by focusing on a downstream team pushing back, an ambiguity question by focusing on unclear ownership, and a failure question by focusing on the rollback decision. The candidate does not need four separate stories; they need one story with clearly identified behavioral segments.

## Common traps

- Preparing one story per expected question instead of 3–5 reusable projects, leaving you blank when the wording changes.
- Choosing stories by company prestige or headline outcome rather than personal involvement, so the answer collapses when asked what you specifically did.
- Reciting the project timeline but spending little time on Actions, so the interviewer cannot assess behavior.
- Treating STAR/R as a fixed script rather than a reorderable structure, making answers sound over-rehearsed and unable to adapt.

</details>

**Question**

**Options**

Orchestration: a central coordinator invokes steps and tracks state; better for complex flows with explicit retries and branching. ## Your 60-second answer

A saga is a way to run a distributed business transaction by splitting it into a sequence of local transactions across services. Each service commits its own database work and then emits an event or message to trigger the next service. If a later step fails, we don't try to roll back globally; instead we run compensating transactions in reverse order to undo the earlier committed changes. For example, in a payment flow: reserve inventory, charge the card, then ship. If shipping fails, refund the card and release the inventory. The reason we use sagas instead of distributed transactions is that two-phase commit blocks resources and doesn't scale across many services. The main tradeoff is that intermediate states are visible—after the card is charged but before shipping succeeds, another request may see a paid order without shipment. So you need idempotency keys and careful compensation logic.

## If they dig deeper

**What are the two ways to coordinate a saga, and how do you choose between them?**

Choreography uses domain events so each service reacts to the previous service's outcome; it fits simple flows with few participants and loose coupling. Orchestration uses a central coordinator that calls services and tracks state; it is better for complex flows because retries, branching, and audit are explicit. Choose orchestration when you need a single place to see status and recover; choose choreography when you want fewer moving parts and services already communicate by events.

**If a later step fails after earlier steps have committed, what exactly happens?**

The saga runs compensating transactions for each previously committed step, in reverse order. For example, a captured payment is refunded and reserved inventory is released. Each compensation is a new business operation, not a database rollback, and it must be idempotent because compensation itself can fail or be retried.

**How do you ensure a payment isn't processed twice in this model?**

You make every step idempotent and use an idempotency key that is persisted with the payment request. Consumers deduplicate events by a unique event ID, and downstream services use unique constraints or check state before acting. For example, a payment service refuses to capture the same idempotency key a second time even if the message is redelivered.

**How do you handle many concurrent transfers to or from the same account?**

Serialize writes per account: use row-level locks or a single partitioned writer per account, or optimistic versioning and retry on conflict. In a ledger design, you insert immutable debit/credit entries rather than updating one balance row, which reduces lock contention and lets you derive balance by summation or materialized view.

**What isolation problems do sagas create because intermediate transactions are committed, and how do you mitigate them?**

A saga can expose dirty reads and lost updates across services: another transaction may read a state that will later be compensated. You can reduce this with semantic locks that mark a resource as pending, version fields to detect changes, or by delaying side effects until the last possible step. You cannot get global ACID isolation; you choose availability and compensate inconsistencies instead.

## Worked example

A checkout saga in an e-commerce system coordinates Inventory, Payment, and Shipping. Step 1: Inventory service starts a local transaction, decrements stock for SKU A-100 from 10 to 9, commits, then publishes InventoryReserved{order_id: o-1}. Step 2: Payment service consumes that event, charges $49.99 to the card in its own transaction, commits, and publishes PaymentCaptured{order_id: o-1, payment_id: p-9}. Step 3: Shipping service tries to create a label, but the warehouse API times out. The orchestrator marks the saga failed and runs compensations in reverse: Payment refunds payment p-9 idempotently; Inventory increments SKU A-100 back to 10. The final state is no order, restored inventory, and refunded card.

## Common traps

- Confusing compensating transactions with automatic rollbacks—compensations are business operations you must design, not free undos.
- Assuming saga provides ACID isolation—intermediate committed states are visible and can cause lost updates unless you add controls.
- Forgetting idempotency—a retried message or callback can charge a customer twice if steps or compensations are not idempotent.
- Reaching for distributed two-phase commit by default—it blocks resources and hurts availability, while sagas trade some consistency for availability and scalability.

</details>

### 68. Microservices · Medium

*system_design · gate confidence 0.8*

<sub>to object to this card: `## sd-microservices` then `match: Classify each communication or data pattern by whether it is`</sub>

**Question**

Classify each communication or data pattern by whether it is synchronous request/reply, asynchronous event-driven, or a shared-database coupling. Assume standard microservices implementations.

**Options**

**Items**: HTTP call to fetch business details per candidate, Publishing a rating_updated event, Multiple services reading the same business table, gRPC call to review service for rating, Consuming events to update a search index, A review service writing directly to the search service's database
**Columns**: Synchronous request/reply, Asynchronous event-driven, Shared-database coupling

**Answer (the reader is graded on)**

- 0 ↔ 0 · 1 ↔ 1 · 2 ↔ 2 · 3 ↔ 0 · 4 ↔ 1 · 5 ↔ 2

**Reference answer**

Synchronous request/reply: HTTP call to fetch business details per candidate, gRPC call to review service for rating. Asynchronous event-driven: publishing a rating_updated event, consuming events to update a search index. Shared-database coupling: multiple services reading the same business table, a review service writing directly to the search service's database.

**Graded on**

- Synchronous calls couple services in the request path and amplify tail latency.
- Asynchronous events decouple services and enable eventual consistency.
- Shared databases block independent deployment and create hidden coupling.

<details><summary>The lesson this came from</summary>

Microservices architecture structures a system as a collection of small, autonomous services, each modeled around a bounded business capability and typically owning its own data store. Services communicate over the network using synchronous protocols such as HTTP/REST or gRPC, or asynchronously through message brokers. Each service can be built, deployed, and scaled independently, which increases agility but introduces distributed-systems complexity.

## Why interviewers ask this

This is often evaluated through 'Design Yelp or Nearby Friends,' a very hard question asked at Amazon, Facebook, Google, and Uber. The interviewer is testing whether you can define service boundaries and data ownership, choose synchronous versus asynchronous communication, and avoid distributed anti-patterns such as synchronous fan-out or shared databases. Follow-ups on spatial indexing, caching, and ranking probe whether you separate the read model from source services.

## The core idea

The core of microservices is decomposition along business capabilities so each team can deploy and scale independently, and that only works when services are autonomous, including data ownership. For proximity search, the request path must not depend on synchronous calls to many services for each candidate. Instead, build a specialized read model such as a search index or materialized view that combines location, category, and pre-aggregated rating, and update it asynchronously from source services. Static and dynamic location are different problems: static places fit geohash or spatial indexing with infrequent updates, while dynamic entities need a high-write location service and possibly pub/sub.

## Key points

- In microservices, each service owns its bounded context and its own database; sharing a database couples services and blocks independent deployment.
- Communication is either synchronous request/reply over HTTP/gRPC or asynchronous events over a broker, and synchronous chains amplify tail latency.
- For static location data, use a geohash or spatial index over a rarely changing set; dynamic locations need a separate high-write store with TTLs.
- Search ranking should happen in a denormalized search index or materialized view containing pre-aggregated ratings and location, not by calling services per candidate.
- Orchestration uses a central coordinator for a workflow, while choreography lets services react to events; orchestration gives visibility, and choreography reduces coupling.

## Your 60-second answer

For a Yelp or Nearby Friends design, I’d decompose this into a business service that owns static place data, a location service that owns geospatial state, and a search service backed by a denormalized search index. The index is the read model: business and review writes are published as events, and an indexer updates the index asynchronously with pre-aggregated ratings and geohashes. On a query, the search service filters candidates by geohash prefix within the radius, scores them locally using distance and rating weights, and returns the top results without calling other services per candidate. The reason is that synchronous fan-out to business and review services for every candidate creates tail latency and a distributed N+1 query. The main trade-off is eventual consistency between the source services and the search index.

## If they dig deeper

**How will you store location data?**

Static business locations fit a geospatial column in the business/search database, such as a geohash with a spatial index or PostGIS. Dynamic user locations are high-churn ephemeral state, so they belong in a separate location service backed by Redis or Cassandra with TTLs, not in the same store as static places.

**Will you use latitude-longitude, geohashing, or a spatial index (e.g., R-Tree, QuadTree)?**

Store latitude and longitude as the source of truth, but index for queries using geohashes or a spatial index. Geohash prefixes allow fast coarse filtering by area; for exact radius queries, filter candidates by neighboring geohash cells then compute haversine distance, or use an R-tree or QuadTree for range queries. The choice depends on read/write ratio and whether updates are static or dynamic.

**How do you handle different types of proximity services - static (e.g., restaurants) vs dynamic (e.g., nearby friends or riders)?**

Static locations are indexed once and updated rarely, so you can precompute geohashes and denormalize them into a search index. Dynamic locations change constantly, so they need a separate high-write location service and cannot rely on the same static spatial index. For dynamic proximity, maintain an in-memory geospatial set per active user or region and refresh it frequently, or use a grid/quadtree with pub/sub for updates.

**What kind of caching would you implement for frequently accessed areas (e.g., popular cities)?**

Cache query results by geohash prefix or bounding box for popular areas, with short TTLs for dynamic results and longer TTLs for static businesses. Invalidate the static cache via events when a business changes. This reduces load on the search index and avoids recomputing top results for dense cities.

**How will you rank and personalize results (e.g., by distance, rating, user preferences)?**

Build a denormalized candidate document in the search index that includes pre-aggregated rating, categories, and location, then apply ranking over that local document set. Combine distance, rating, and personalization signals in a scoring function, but materialize the expensive signal aggregations ahead of time rather than calling business or review services in the request path.

## Worked example

A search request asks for restaurants within 2 km. The search service converts the user location to a geohash prefix and queries the search index for candidate documents in neighboring prefix cells. Each document already carries its business ID, geohash, category, and an aggregated average rating maintained by an event from the reviews service. The search service computes haversine distance for each candidate, scores it as 0.7*(1 - distance/radius) + 0.3*(rating/5), and returns the top 20. When a new review arrives, the reviews service publishes a rating_updated event; an indexer consumes it and updates that one document. The request path never calls the business or review service per candidate.

## Common traps

- Treating microservices as merely splitting code by entity while still sharing a database, which recreates coupling and blocks independent deployment.
- Building a synchronous request path that calls the business or review service for every candidate within a radius, creating a distributed N+1 query and high tail latency.
- Using the same storage and indexing strategy for static businesses and dynamic friends, causing write amplification and stale spatial indexes.
- Deploying microservices without idempotent consumers and retries; duplicate events from at-least-once brokers then corrupt state or repeat side effects.

</details>

### 69. Design a news feed · Easy

*system_design · gate confidence 0.8*

<sub>to object to this card: `## sd-design-a-news-feed` then `match: Classify each item by the layer of the news feed system wher`</sub>

**Question**

Classify each item by the layer of the news feed system where it primarily belongs: Write Path, Read Path, or Shared/Supporting. Items are shuffled.

**Options**

**Items**: Fanout to follower timelines, Feed assembly, Post storage, Ranking, Asynchronous queues, User graph storage, Feed caching, CDN media delivery
**Columns**: Write Path, Read Path, Shared/Supporting

**Answer (the reader is graded on)**

- 0 ↔ 0 · 1 ↔ 1 · 2 ↔ 2 · 3 ↔ 1 · 4 ↔ 0 · 5 ↔ 2 · 6 ↔ 1 · 7 ↔ 2

**Reference answer**

Fanout to follower timelines and asynchronous queues belong to the write path; feed assembly, ranking, and feed caching belong to the read path; post storage, user graph storage, and CDN media delivery are shared or supporting layers used by both paths.

**Graded on**

- Write path handles post creation and distribution to follower timelines.
- Read path assembles and ranks candidate posts into a feed.
- Post storage and user graph storage are shared data stores used by both paths.
- CDN media delivery is a supporting layer that serves media independently of feed logic.

<details><summary>The lesson this came from</summary>

A news feed system aggregates content created by accounts a user follows, ranks the content, and serves it as a paginated list. The write path stores new posts and distributes them to follower timelines; the read path assembles a feed from stored or pulled candidate posts. Core components include post storage, user graph storage, feed generation, ranking, caching, and media delivery via CDN.

## Why interviewers ask this

Interviewers ask this to test whether you can handle a read-heavy, fanout-heavy system with huge variance in follower counts. They probe your ability to choose between push and pull models, design caching, model data, and explain trade-offs between latency, consistency, and write amplification. This question is known from Facebook/Meta and Instagram design loops.

## The core idea

A news feed is a read-heavy system: reads outnumber writes by roughly 100:1 in typical designs. For ordinary users, fanout on write (push) precomputes follower timelines so reads are fast; for celebrities, fanout on read (pull) avoids writing to millions of timelines. Ranking is not just reverse chronological—it scores candidates by recency, affinity, and engagement. Caching and precomputation absorb most read load, while asynchronous fanout and partitioning absorb write load. The central trade-off is read latency vs write amplification and freshness.

## Key points

- For ordinary users with up to a few thousand followers, push-based fanout writes each new post to the follower timelines at post time, making feed reads O(1) or simple cache lookups.
- For accounts with millions of followers, pull-based fanout avoids massive write amplification; their posts are merged into follower feeds at read time instead of written to each timeline.
- Feed ranking uses candidate generation from followed accounts, then scoring by factors like recency, affinity, engagement, and content type, not just chronology.
- Reads dominate: typical designs assume a 100:1 read-to-write ratio; caching hot feeds in Redis/Memcached with LRU and serving media via CDN reduces database and origin load.
- Data is sharded by user ID or post ID, with asynchronous fanout queues and batch writes to handle spikes and eventual consistency across follower timelines.

## Your 60-second answer

A news feed system needs to store posts and serve each user a personalized, ranked list of content from accounts they follow. The core decision is fanout. For ordinary users, I'd push each new post to the follower timelines at write time: the post ID is appended to a cached list for each follower, so reads are fast. For celebrities with millions of followers, I'd not fan out on write; instead, I'd pull their recent posts at read time and merge them into the follower's feed. I'd rank the candidate posts using a scoring model based on recency, affinity, engagement, and content type, then return the top few hundred. Reads are cached with LRU and CDNs; writes are processed asynchronously through queues and batched. The main trade-off is latency versus consistency: push gives low-latency reads but eventual consistency during fanout.

## If they dig deeper

**How will you handle fanout: push model, pull model, or hybrid?**

Use a hybrid. For normal users with up to a few thousand followers, push the post to each follower's timeline storage or cache at write time, because read latency is more important and the fanout cost is bounded. For accounts with millions of followers, do not push; instead pull their recent posts at read time and merge them into the feed, avoiding write amplification. Optionally push to recently active followers and let inactive followers pull on next login.

**How does the system change for a user with millions of friends/followers?**

For a celebrity, pushing one post to all followers would generate millions of timeline writes, so the write path must be changed. Store celebrity posts in a separate timeline or post list and merge them at read time for each follower. If we want lower read latency for active users, we can maintain a hybrid: push to a subset of recently active followers and have the rest pull, possibly with a cap on fanout size.

**How will you fetch and score new content at scale - especially when a user opens the app after days?**

The read service generates the feed lazily on first open: it pulls recent posts from each followed account or from the user's precomputed timeline cache, merges them, and passes candidates to a ranker. For a dormant user, there is no continuously updated timeline; we compute the feed on demand and cache the result for a short time. Ranking must consider recency and user affinity so older posts from close friends can still appear above newer, less relevant posts, rather than a strict reverse-chronological order.

**How will you handle the scalability of writes and reads - e.g., batching, caching, partitioning?**

Writes go through an asynchronous fanout service that batches timeline inserts and partitions work by user ID or shard; this smooths spikes when a popular user posts. Reads are served from distributed caches like Redis or Memcached with LRU eviction, backed by read replicas of the database. Media is offloaded to object storage and served via CDN, so the feed service only handles metadata. Pagination limits response size and reduces load.

## Worked example

Assume a system with 500M daily active users, 95M photo posts and 5M video posts per day, and a 100:1 read-to-write ratio. For write fanout: if a normal user with 300 followers posts one photo, the fanout service must insert that post ID into 300 follower timeline caches. If the system handles 500 post writes per second, that is 150,000 timeline writes per second, which can be done by batching inserts across shards. For a celebrity with 50M followers, the same fanout would require 50M timeline inserts per post, so the system does not push; it stores the post once and, at read time, merges the celebrity's recent posts into each follower's feed. A returning user who follows 500 accounts triggers a read that fetches recent post IDs from those accounts, ranks them by recency and affinity, and returns the top 200. With 50,000 feed requests per second, caching precomputed feeds for active users in Redis and serving media from a CDN can reduce database reads by an order of magnitude.

## Common traps

- Proposing only push-based fanout for all users; with celebrity accounts this causes massive write amplification and can delay post visibility for hours.
- Designing the feed as strictly reverse chronological; real news feeds rank by relevance, so ignoring ranking and personalization misses a core requirement.
- Jumping to a final architecture without estimating read/write volume or identifying bottlenecks; interviewers expect iterative scaling based on load.
- Storing media in the same relational database as post metadata; images and videos must go to object storage and CDN, not bloat the primary database.

</details>

### 70. Builder Pattern · Medium

*lld · gate confidence 0.8*

<sub>to object to this card: `## lld-builder-pattern` then `match: Classify each statement about the Builder pattern as belongi`</sub>

**Question**

Classify each statement about the Builder pattern as belonging to the Builder, the Product, or the Director.

**Options**

**Items**: Accumulates configuration and validates it in build(), Is immutable and returned by build(), Sequences construction steps, May be shared safely across threads, Should not be shared across threads, Centralizes cross-field validation
**Columns**: Builder, Product, Director

**Answer (the reader is graded on)**

- 0 ↔ 0 · 1 ↔ 1 · 2 ↔ 2 · 3 ↔ 1 · 4 ↔ 0 · 5 ↔ 0

**Reference answer**

The Builder accumulates configuration and validates it in build(); the Product is the immutable result; the Director sequences construction steps.

**Graded on**

- Builder is mutable and accumulates configuration.
- Product is immutable and returned by build().
- Director sequences builder steps.

<details><summary>The lesson this came from</summary>

Builder encapsulates the construction steps of an object behind a fluent API. Clients call named methods to set individual fields, then call build() to receive a fully constructed product, often immutable. This separates the construction process from the product's representation, letting the same steps create different configurations without exposing long constructors or half-initialized states. In the classic GoF form, a Director may invoke the builder's steps in a fixed sequence to create different representations.

## Why interviewers ask this

Interviewers ask this to see whether a candidate can design APIs for objects with many optional or interdependent parameters. It tests understanding of invariants, immutability, and separating construction from representation. They also look for judgment about when extra builder code is worth it over setters or multiple constructors.

## The core idea

A builder is a mutable helper that accumulates configuration, validates it, and returns an immutable product from build(). This removes the need for telescoping constructors and catches invalid states at build time rather than halfway through field-by-field setup. The key separation is that the construction steps can be varied independently of the object's final representation. Strong implementations declare product fields final, copy defensive collections, and centralize cross-field validation in build(). Builders are not automatically thread-safe; they are typically used locally on one thread, while the resulting immutable product can be shared safely.

## Key points

- Builder replaces a long list of positional constructor arguments with named fluent methods, preventing errors from swapped parameters.
- The build() method is the central point for validation and for constructing the product with all invariants satisfied.
- In the classic GoF pattern, a Director sequences builder steps, enabling the same construction process to yield different product representations.
- A builder is a mutable object and should not be shared across threads; the product it returns can be immutable and safely shared.
- Defensive copies are required for collection fields, otherwise callers can mutate the contents of an 'immutable' product after build().

## Your 60-second answer

The builder pattern separates the construction of a complex object from its representation. Instead of a constructor with many positional parameters, you create a builder object with a named method for each optional part; each method returns the builder so calls can chain, and a final build() method returns the finished immutable product. It is useful when a class has several optional or interdependent parameters, or when one construction process should produce different configurations. The main reason it beats a long constructor is readability and safety: callers can no longer swap two integers, and validation can happen in build() before the object exists. The trade-off is more code: you need to write and maintain the builder class and keep it synchronized with the product fields. I would reach for it when the constructor becomes unwieldy or when invariants span multiple fields.

## If they dig deeper

**How does Builder improve on a plain constructor or setter-based initialization?**

A constructor with many positional parameters forces callers to get every argument exactly right and becomes unreadable; setters allow an object to be used before it is fully initialized. Builder supplies named methods for readable setup, can enforce all invariants in build(), and returns an immutable product that never exists half-configured.

**Where should validation live in a builder?**

Individual setters can reject invalid values immediately, but cross-field rules must be checked in build() because only at that point is the complete configuration known. build() should throw an exception such as IllegalArgumentException or IllegalStateException and must not return a partially built product.

**What is the Director's role in the classic GoF Builder?**

A Director takes a Builder interface and invokes its construction methods in a specific order to assemble a product. This lets the same algorithm create different representations by swapping the concrete builder, and it keeps sequencing logic out of the client.

**How would you use Builder to produce an immutable object that contains a mutable collection?**

The builder's collection setters should copy the caller's list defensively, and the product should store an unmodifiable view or a defensive copy of that collection. A common mistake is storing the original list reference, which lets callers mutate the 'immutable' object after build().

**How does inheritance affect fluent builder design?**

A base class builder that returns its own type breaks chaining when a subclass adds methods, because those methods can no longer be called after a base method returns. The standard fix is a recursive generic self-type parameter (class Builder<T extends Builder<T>>) with each method returning T, or to avoid extending the builder and duplicate the needed fields.

## Worked example

Consider a NetworkConfig with host, port, timeoutMillis, retries, and useTls. A positional constructor call such as NetworkConfig("db.internal", 5432, 5000, 3, true) gives no hint which integer is the timeout. The builder version reads NetworkConfig.builder().host("db.internal").port(5432).timeoutMillis(5000).retries(3).useTls(true).build(); each method name makes the mapping explicit. The build() method checks that port is between 1 and 65535 and timeoutMillis is positive; if the check fails, it throws and no partially built object is created. The product's constructor is private, assigns all fields once as final references, and returns an immutable object.

## Common traps

- Returning a new builder from each setter instead of this; the chain compiles but each call starts a fresh builder, so earlier settings are lost.
- Validating only inside individual setters; cross-field rules like a timeout being meaningful only with a configured endpoint are missed.
- Exposing collections by reference from the product; callers can mutate a list after build and break immutability.

</details>

## Tap the bug (`tap-the-bug` · tap_in_place)

### 71. Heap / Priority Queue · Medium

*dsa · gate confidence 0.7*

<sub>to object to this card: `## heap-priority-queue` then `match: You are reviewing a Java method that finds the kth largest e`</sub>

**Question**

You are reviewing a Java method that finds the kth largest element in an array using a min-heap of size k. Which line contains the bug?

**Options**

A. PriorityQueue<Integer> minHeap = new PriorityQueue<>();
B. for (int num : nums) {
C.     if (minHeap.size() < k) {
D.         minHeap.offer(num);
E.     } else if (num < minHeap.peek()) {
F.         minHeap.poll();
G.         minHeap.offer(num);
H.     }
I. }
J. return minHeap.peek();

**Answer (the reader is graded on)**

- Correct: E.     } else if (num < minHeap.peek()) {

**Reference answer**

Line 4 is the bug: the comparison is reversed. To keep the k largest elements in a min-heap, you should replace the root only when the new element is greater than the root. Using 'less than' discards larger elements and keeps smaller ones, so the heap ends up containing the k smallest elements, and the root becomes the kth smallest, not the kth largest.

**Graded on**

- For kth largest, maintain a min-heap of size k containing the k largest candidates.
- The root of a min-heap is the smallest among the kept elements, which is exactly the kth largest.
- A new element should replace the root only if it is greater than the root.
- The buggy comparison keeps smaller elements, turning the heap into a container of the k smallest.

<details><summary>The lesson this came from</summary>

A binary heap is a complete binary tree, usually stored in an array, where every parent is <= its children in a min-heap or >= its children in a max-heap. The root is always the minimum or maximum element, readable in O(1); inserting an element or removing the root restores the heap property in O(log n). A priority queue is the abstract data type that returns elements by priority rather than arrival order, and heaps are its standard implementation. Default ordering differs by language: Java's PriorityQueue is a min-heap, C++ std::priority_queue is a max-heap, and Python's heapq provides min-heap functions on a list.

## Why interviewers ask this

Interviewers use heap problems to test whether you recognize repeated min/max queries over a changing collection and avoid sorting every time. Top-k, two-heap median, and k-way merge questions appear at companies like Meta, Apple, Spotify, Roblox, and Citadel. Strong answers show the correct heap orientation, when to bound heap size, and the difference between O(n) heap construction and O(log n) updates.

## The core idea

When a collection changes and the next operation is 'give me the smallest or largest so far', a heap keeps that extremum at the root with O(1) access and O(log n) updates. For top-k, keep a heap of size k: to find the kth largest, use a min-heap of the k largest candidates and discard anything smaller than the root. For median tracking, split the data into a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, rebalancing after each insert. For merging multiple sorted streams, place the current head of each stream in a min-heap, pop the smallest, then push that stream's next element. The central choice is usually which heap orientation and size constraint make the desired rank directly accessible.

## Key points

- A binary heap is a complete binary tree satisfying the heap property; in a 0-indexed array, the children of index i are 2i+1 and 2i+2.
- Insert and delete-min/max are O(log n); building a heap from n arbitrary elements by heapify is O(n), and reading the root is O(1).
- A priority queue is an abstract data type that removes elements by priority, not arrival order, and a heap is its standard implementation.
- For top-k, maintain a heap of size k: use a min-heap of the k largest for kth largest, and a max-heap of the k smallest for kth smallest.
- In Java, PriorityQueue is a min-heap by default; in C++, std::priority_queue is a max-heap by default; Python's heapq implements a min-heap on lists.

## Your 60-second answer

A heap is a complete binary tree where every parent is <= or >= its children, so the root is the minimum or maximum. That gives O(1) access to the extremum and O(log n) insertion and deletion. A priority queue is the abstract interface that returns elements by priority, and a heap is the standard implementation. I reach for it when a collection keeps changing and I need the largest or smallest item repeatedly—top-k, scheduling, merging sorted streams, or tracking a median. For the kth largest I keep a min-heap of size k: each incoming element is compared with the root; if larger, I replace the root. The root is then the kth largest because it is the smallest of the k largest kept. For median, I split into a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half and rebalance after each insert. The tradeoff is that a heap only exposes the extremum efficiently, not arbitrary order or search.

## If they dig deeper

**How is a priority queue different from a normal FIFO queue?**

A FIFO queue removes elements in the order they arrived, regardless of their values. A priority queue removes the element with the highest or lowest priority first, so arrival order is not the deciding factor. Heaps implement priority queues because they can expose and update the extremum in logarithmic time.

**Why maintain only k elements in top-k instead of sorting the whole array?**

Sorting costs O(n log n) time and typically O(n) or O(log n) auxiliary space. A size-k heap costs O(n log k) time and O(k) space, which is better when k is much smaller than n. It also adapts naturally to a stream: each new element requires only O(log k) work to update the answer.

**Walk through the two-heap median structure.**

Keep a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half. After each insertion, rebalance so heap sizes differ by at most one, and ensure every lower half element is <= every upper half element. If total size is odd, the median is the top of the larger heap; if even, it is the average of the two heap tops.

**For Find Median from Data Stream, if all numbers are guaranteed to fall in [0,100], how would you optimize?**

Maintain an array of 101 counts and a running total. Each add increments one count in O(1). To find the median, walk the counts until reaching ceil(total/2), and for an even total continue to the next non-zero bucket to compute the average.

**If 99% of the numbers are in [0,100] but the rest can be anywhere, how would you optimize median tracking?**

Keep a 101-slot histogram for the [0,100] range and a separate rank-capable structure for outliers below 0 and above 100. Track total counts per region. To find the median, locate the middle index by skipping the below-zero region, then the histogram, then the above-100 region, which keeps the common case fast while still handling rare extreme values.

## Worked example

Find the 2nd largest in nums = [3,2,1,5,6,4]. Keep a min-heap of size 2. Process 3: heap is [3]. Process 2: heap is [2,3], root is 2. Process 1: root 2 is larger than 1, so discard 1. Process 5: root 2 is smaller than 5, so pop 2 and push 5; heap is [3,5]. Process 6: root 3 is smaller than 6, so pop 3 and push 6; heap is [5,6]. Process 4: root 5 is larger than 4, so discard 4. The root, 5, is the 2nd largest. The heap contains the two largest elements seen so far, and the root is the smaller of those two, which is exactly the kth largest.

## Common traps

- Using a max-heap of size k for kth largest and reporting its root: the root is the largest element, not the kth largest.
- Forgetting that building a heap from n arbitrary elements is O(n), not O(n log n); heapify is linear.
- Mixing up language defaults: Java's PriorityQueue is a min-heap, while C++ std::priority_queue is a max-heap by default.
- Returning the median in a two-heap structure without first rebalancing; one heap can drift and its top no longer represents the middle.

</details>

### 72. Library Management System Design · Medium

*lld · gate confidence 0.8*

<sub>to object to this card: `## lld-library-management-system-design` then `match: A candidate proposes the following checkout method for the L`</sub>

**Question**

A candidate proposes the following checkout method for the Library Management System. Which line contains the bug?

```
1  def checkout(member, book_item):
2      if member.active_loans.count() >= 5:
3          raise LimitExceededError
4      if book_item.status != 'AVAILABLE':
5          raise ItemUnavailableError
6      loan = Loan(member=member, book_item=book_item,
7                  checkout_date=today, due_date=today + 10 days)
8      book_item.status = 'CHECKED_OUT'
9      loan.save()
10     book_item.save()
```

**Options**

A. 1  def checkout(member, book_item):
B. 2      if member.active_loans.count() >= 5:
C. 3          raise LimitExceededError
D. 4      if book_item.status != 'AVAILABLE':
E. 5          raise ItemUnavailableError
F. 6      loan = Loan(member=member, book_item=book_item,
G. 7                  checkout_date=today, due_date=today + 10 days)
H. 8      book_item.status = 'CHECKED_OUT'
I. 9      loan.save()
J. 10     book_item.save()

**Answer (the reader is graded on)**

- Correct: B. 2      if member.active_loans.count() >= 5:

**Reference answer**

Line 2 is the bug: the member's active loan count is checked before the transaction begins, so two concurrent checkouts can both pass the check and exceed the limit of five. The count and the loan creation must happen atomically inside a transaction with row locking or a conditional update.

**Graded on**

- The 5-loan limit must be enforced atomically with the loan creation.
- Checking the count outside a transaction allows a race condition.
- A transaction with row locking or a conditional update prevents exceeding the limit.

<details><summary>The lesson this came from</summary>

A Library Management System LLD defines classes and interactions to manage book inventory, member accounts, and lending. The core model separates Book (title, author, subject, ISBN, publication date) from BookItem (physical copy with barcode and rack number). Loan/Checkout records which member has which copy, with checkout and due dates; Reservation tracks waiting members; fine transactions handle overdue returns. Services enforce rules such as max 5 active loans and 10-day loan period.

## Why interviewers ask this

Interviewers test whether you can identify entity boundaries, especially the difference between catalog metadata and a physical copy. They look for enforcement of business rules like loan limits, due dates, and fines, and for handling of concurrent requests such as two members trying to borrow the same copy. They also expect requirement clarification questions about search, reservations, and notifications.

## The core idea

The essential abstraction is Book vs BookItem. A Book stores searchable metadata and may have many BookItems. Loan binds a Member to a BookItem at checkout time; due date is calculated from checkout date plus loan period, max 10 days in requirements. A central LendingService validates atomically: item is available, member has fewer than 5 active loans, then creates Loan. Reservations are per Book, not per copy; when a copy is returned, the next reservation is notified and the copy becomes available. Fines are calculated on return if returnDate > dueDate, using a configurable daily rate. This separation keeps search and physical inventory independent and allows extending rules.

## Key points

- A Book stores title, author, subject, ISBN, and publication date; each physical copy is a separate BookItem with unique barcode and rack number.
- A Member can have at most 5 active checkouts at once, and each loan has a maximum period of 10 days from checkout.
- Loan/Checkout record holds member, book item, checkout date, due date, and optional return date; overdue fines are applied when return date exceeds due date.
- Reservations are placed on a Book when no copy is available, and notifications are sent when a copy is returned or a loan becomes overdue.
- Search is performed against Book metadata, not physical copies, so multiple copies appear as one search result.

## Your 60-second answer

I’d design it around five entities: Book, BookItem, Member, Loan, and Reservation. Book is catalog metadata; BookItem is a physical copy with a barcode and rack number. Loan connects a Member to a BookItem and stores checkout date and due date. The lending rules sit in a service: a member can’t have more than five active loans, and each loan is due in ten days. If a book has no available copies, a member creates a Reservation; when a copy returns, the system notifies the next waiting member. Fines are calculated at return by comparing the return date to the due date. Search runs on Book metadata. The main trade-off: putting rules in a service rather than inside entities makes enforcement transactional and easier to change, but it means entities themselves don’t protect their invariants.

## If they dig deeper

**How do you model multiple copies of the same title?**

Split Book and BookItem. Book holds title, author, subject, ISBN, and publication date for search; BookItem holds a unique barcode and rack number, plus a reference to its Book. Availability and loan state live on BookItem, while reservations and catalog search are handled at the Book level.

**How would you enforce the maximum five active checkouts and avoid race conditions?**

Use a transaction around the checkout operation. Inside it, count the member’s active loans, verify it is below five, verify the target BookItem is available, then insert the Loan and mark the item checked out. Database row locking or conditional updates prevent two concurrent checkouts from both succeeding on the same copy or exceeding the limit.

**How do reservations work when a book is unavailable?**

A Reservation is an entity linking a Member to a Book, with a timestamp and status. Reservations are queued per Book. When a Loan is returned, the system checks if any active reservations exist for that title, notifies the earliest one, and the reserved copy is not available for general checkout until the reservation is processed or expires.

**How do you calculate and collect fines?**

On return, if the return date is after the due date, create a FineTransaction for the overdue days multiplied by a configurable daily rate. The FineTransaction references the loan and member, and payment updates mark it paid. A common extension is to block checkout if a member has unpaid fines above a threshold, but that policy should be confirmed.

**How would you handle notifications reliably at scale?**

Use an asynchronous outbox pattern: when a loan is returned or becomes overdue, write the notification event in the same transaction as the state change, then a background worker publishes it to a queue. Consumers send email/SMS/push and record delivery, with idempotency keys so redelivery doesn’t duplicate messages.

## Worked example

Suppose Book 'Clean Code' has two BookItems: B001 and B002. Member Alice currently has four active loans and checks out B001 on day 0; the system sets due date to day 10 because the policy max is 10 days. On day 12 Alice returns B001; the system calculates two days overdue and creates a FineTransaction for 2 * configuredDailyFine. Meanwhile Bob had reserved the title while both copies were checked out; when B001 is returned, the reservation service notifies Bob. Bob then checks out B001, and his loan gets day 0 checkout date and day 10 due date.

## Common traps

- Modeling only a Book without BookItem makes it impossible to track individual copies, their availability, or barcodes.
- Putting business rules like the 5-item limit only in the UI allows API clients to bypass them; enforcement belongs in the service layer.
- Ignoring concurrency can let two members check out the same BookItem simultaneously if availability is not checked atomically.
- Confusing reservation with checkout: a reservation should hold a place in line, not assign a specific copy until one is available.

</details>

### 73. Load balancing · Medium

*system_design · gate confidence 0.7*

<sub>to object to this card: `## sd-load-balancing` then `match: A load balancer distributes traffic across three backend ser`</sub>

**Question**

A load balancer distributes traffic across three backend servers using the following configuration. Which line is the bottleneck that will cause uneven load distribution under a workload of long-lived, variable-duration connections?

**Options**

A. algorithm: round_robin
B. health_check: enabled
C. servers: [A, B, C]
D. layer: L4

**Answer (the reader is graded on)**

- Correct: A. algorithm: round_robin

**Reference answer**

Line 3 is the bottleneck. Round robin cycles through servers without considering active connection counts, so with long-lived connections of varying duration, it can pile many connections onto one server while others sit idle. Least connections would adapt to the current load.

**Graded on**

- Round robin assumes uniform request duration and server capacity.
- Long-lived, variable-duration connections make round robin distribute unevenly.
- Least connections selects the server with the fewest active connections.

<details><summary>The lesson this came from</summary>

Load balancing distributes incoming network or application traffic across multiple backend servers using a configurable algorithm and health checks. It prevents a single server from becoming a bottleneck, improves throughput and response time, and enables horizontal scaling by adding or removing servers without changing clients. Load balancers can operate at Layer 4 (transport, TCP/UDP) or Layer 7 (application, HTTP).

## Why interviewers ask this

Interviewers use load balancing to test whether you can design for scale, availability, and failure handling. They expect you to choose an algorithm for the workload, explain where balancing happens in a multi-tier architecture, and describe how health checks and failover keep the system online.

## The core idea

A load balancer sits in front of a pool of servers and chooses which server receives each request based on an algorithm. It stops serving unhealthy instances and lets you add or remove capacity without disrupting clients. The algorithm matters less than correct health checking and the distinction between Layer 4 (connection-level) and Layer 7 (request/content-level) routing. For stateful workloads you may need session affinity; for uneven server capacity, weighted algorithms.

## Key points

- A health check marks backend instances as healthy or unhealthy; the load balancer routes only to healthy instances and can trigger failover.
- Round robin cycles sequentially and suits uniform, stateless servers; weighted round robin adds capacity weights.
- Least connections sends a new request to the server with the fewest active connections and adapts to uneven workloads.
- Layer 4 load balancers route using IP and TCP/UDP data, while Layer 7 load balancers inspect HTTP headers, cookies, or paths.
- High availability requires the load balancer itself to be redundant, often via active-passive pairs or multiple load balancers with DNS failover.

## Your 60-second answer

A load balancer sits in front of backend servers and distributes incoming requests across them. It avoids overloading one machine, keeps latency low, and lets the system tolerate server failures. The balancer uses periodic health checks to take unhealthy servers out of rotation, and an algorithm to select a target: round robin, least connections, or IP hash are common. Layer 4 balancers route on connection-level data, while Layer 7 balancers can inspect HTTP and route by path or cookie. The main trade-off is that the load balancer adds an extra hop and can become a single point of failure, so production systems deploy it in pairs or rely on managed cloud balancers.

## If they dig deeper

**What is the difference between Layer 4 and Layer 7 load balancing?**

Layer 4 balances using transport-layer data like IP addresses and TCP/UDP ports, without inspecting payload, so it is fast and works for any TCP/UDP protocol. Layer 7 terminates and inspects HTTP, enabling routing by URL path, headers, or cookies, and can also handle TLS termination, but uses more CPU.

**How do health checks work, and what happens when an instance fails?**

Active health checks periodically send TCP, HTTP, or gRPC probes to each backend; passive checks infer health from actual request outcomes. After a configured number of failures, the load balancer marks the instance unhealthy and removes it from rotation, so new requests go to healthy servers; it re-adds the instance once checks pass again.

**Which algorithm would you choose for a service with long-lived connections of varying duration?**

Least connections or least response time is better because round robin can accidentally pile many long-lived connections onto one server. A Layer 4 least-connections balancer works well for raw TCP; if content-based routing is needed, use a Layer 7 balancer with HTTP metrics.

**How do you maintain session state when users need to stay on the same server?**

You can use session affinity, or sticky sessions, via a cookie or IP hash so a user returns to the same backend. This hurts even distribution and failover, so the stronger approach is to keep sessions in a shared store such as Redis and let any server serve the request.

**How do you make the load balancer itself highly available?**

Deploy at least two load balancers in an active-passive or active-active pair, share a virtual IP using VRRP or a cloud service, and use health checks between the balancers so a standby takes over automatically. DNS can also point to multiple balancers, and anycast can route clients to the nearest healthy one.

## Worked example

Three servers sit behind a load balancer. With round robin and all healthy, requests 1 through 9 are assigned A, B, C, A, B, C, A, B, C. Now suppose each request holds its connection for a different length of time: A is handling 5 active requests, B 2, and C 0. A least-connections balancer sends the next request to C because it has the fewest current connections, even though round robin might have pointed to A. If C then fails, health checks mark it unhealthy after repeated failed probes and remove it from the pool, so traffic is distributed only across A and B until C passes checks again.

## Common traps

- Choosing an algorithm only for fairness without accounting for variable request duration or heterogeneous server capacity.
- Forgetting that the load balancer itself is a single point of failure unless deployed redundantly.
- Using IP-hash or sticky sessions as a substitute for shared session storage, which breaks failover and horizontal scaling.
- Ignoring health checks: a balancer that routes to a dead instance will still send user traffic and cause errors.

</details>
